analysis.one_liner: Requires mediation and binding arbitration to settle disputes over a first union contract.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in a House committee after sitting for over a year.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers vote to form a union, the employer must negotiate a first contract with them, but the law sets no deadline, and employers can negotiate endlessly without ever signing one. This bill would set a clock: if no first contract is reached within 60 days, a mediator steps in, and 30 days later any unresolved issues go to a neutral arbitrator whose decision is binding on both sides. It amends the National Labor Relations Act, the federal law governing union-management relations.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at newly unionized workplaces, who would get a signed first contract with wages and conditions instead of open-ended negotiations that can drag on for years. Unions gain a way to convert a union election win into an actual contract.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the employer and the union to submit their disagreements to mediation if they have not reached a first contract within 60 days of the union being certified.

If mediation does not produce an agreement within 30 more days, either side can send the remaining disputes to the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service for binding arbitration, meaning a neutral arbitrator's decision becomes the contract.

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing a union election lose the ability to stall indefinitely, since unresolved issues would ultimately be decided by an arbitrator. Federal mediation and arbitration costs are modest.

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration of first contracts takes the terms of a contract out of the hands of the employer and the union and hands them to a third-party arbitrator, which critics argue weakens genuine collective bargaining and imposes terms neither side chose.

The bill imposes a tight timetable — 60 days to a deal or a mediator, and arbitration 30 days after that — which opponents would say pressures employers and unions into rushed decisions on complex workplace terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who have won a union election, the benefit is large: a legal guarantee that negotiations end in an actual contract rather than dragging on indefinitely, which is the most common way a new union ends up with nothing. The cost is a real one — some contract terms would be set by an arbitrator rather than agreed by the parties — but it applies only when the sides cannot agree on their own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Gene Green introduced the bill on November 6, 1997, joined by 25 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On December 10, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it sat.
No further action appears in the record for the rest of the 105th Congress, which ended January 3, 1999; the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers opposed to mandatory first-contract arbitration are better off, since they face no such requirement, and the bill simply expired without any vote ever being held.

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require mediation and binding arbitration of first-contract disputes.

for.name: 25 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Minority Whip David Bonior
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced; 26 total Democrats cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the referral the day the bill was introduced and never reported it out or scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill died in a committee chaired by the opposing party without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill removes their main advantage in first-contract talks — the ability to stall until workers give up — by putting unresolved issues before a binding arbitrator. Under current law an employer can negotiate for years without ever signing a contract.

Unions would win a reliable path from a union election win to a signed first contract, and workers who organize would be more likely to see real results, which also strengthens unions' ability to recruit.
The agency would take on new mediation and arbitration work under the bill's mandatory timetable.
